attacks.claim: Automated SMS to ~142,000 purchased voter-file mobile numbers, plus three reminders, likely lacks prior express consent required for automated texts under TCPA; voter registration is not consent. No legal review, sender registration (10DLC), or voter-file data-use agreement is planned, and STOP handling does not cure an unconsented initial send.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio and send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) with a link to the first poll, then 3 automated reminders over 10 days." / "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out." ABSENT: consent basis, 10DLC registration, legal review, data-use agreement with County Clerk.

attacks.claim: The public CC-BY CSV publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking and created_at per response. In a mid-size city these quasi-identifiers can re-identify individuals; removing resident_id does not anonymize rows, and copies cannot be recalled once published.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Demographics (birth_year, gender, zip, address) collected at optional verification for jury-pool balance reports are reused in a public poll export. This is a purpose change without stated notice or consent.
attacks.evidence: "Verified residents already have address, zip, birth_year, gender (collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports)."

attacks.claim: The weekly public CC-BY export is irreversible and grows each week, while staff cannot edit or delete responses. The plan has no retraction, redaction, correction, or resident-removal path, and no dry run or kill switch before publication.
attacks.evidence: "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)" / "Staff cannot edit or delete responses" / "Week 5: ... launch."

attacks.claim: Mass-texting every registered voter to drive participation conflicts with the agreed anonymous-first, verification-optional constraint and makes participation feel compulsory. This is a product-direction decision the plan does not reconcile, and it must be resolved by the decision owner before build.
attacks.evidence: "Agreed constraint: the product is anonymous-first — residents can participate without verifying identity, and verification is always optional." vs "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)"

attacks.claim: The abuse controls rely on device fingerprints and per-IP limits that are easily evaded (cleared storage, rotating IPs, proxies). The 3/min rule queues rather than rejects, the review queue has no reviewer or capacity, and the data model has no fingerprint or IP field, so the control is unspecified and creates an undocumented linkable identifier store.
attacks.evidence: "1 response per poll per device fingerprint + 1 per verified resident; unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review." / ABSENT: fingerprint or IP field in data model, reviewer, queue capacity.

attacks.claim: The claim that the verified/unverified split stops a brigade is overstated. The 'all responses' column is still a headline figure that a brigade moves; the split changes presentation, not prevention.
attacks.evidence: "Results always show verified and unverified tallies separately, so a brigade of unverified responses cannot masquerade as verified sentiment."

attacks.claim: IRV tie-breaking, exhausted-ballot handling, partial-ranking rules, and ward-to-city aggregation are unspecified, and ward is self-selected for unverified users, so per-ward tallies can be skewed by choice of ward. No tally test plan exists.
attacks.evidence: "results are shown per ward with instant-runoff tallies" / "ward is self-selected for unverified users" / ABSENT: tie, exhausted-ballot, partial-ranking, aggregation rules, tally tests.

attacks.claim: Freezing options on the first response has an unspecified race under concurrent first writes and no defined close-time cutoff.
attacks.evidence: "poll options are frozen once the first response arrives"

attacks.claim: The 'centerpiece' framing is contradicted by the plan's own survey: only 9% wanted polls, while 61% wanted voting records and reasons. No prototype or user test supports building polls first.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" versus "is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: The top request (member voting record with reasons, 61%) and the second (neighborhood alerts, 44%) appear nowhere in sections 2 or 7, so the build may address the lowest-ranked need.
attacks.evidence: "See how my council member voted on each item, and their stated reason — 61%" (absent from sections 2 and 7)

attacks.claim: A ~142,000-recipient burst plus reminders concentrates traffic on one link at send time with no send-rate throttle, queue, or carrier throttling plan, and the 5k-concurrent load target is not derived from this spike.
attacks.evidence: "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)" with "load test (target 5k concurrent)"

attacks.claim: Roughly 568,000 Twilio messages (142k × 4 touches), carrier fees, and 10DLC registration are unbudgeted, with no spend cap or alert. The only stated cost is the $400 file.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)."

attacks.claim: No retry, idempotency, duplicate-send prevention across reminders, invalid-number handling, or alerting is specified for the SMS pipeline, the weekly export, or the Monday staff PDF.
attacks.evidence: "Week 4: open-data export, staff PDF, voter-file import + SMS pipeline." / ABSENT: failure handling, monitoring.

attacks.claim: No retention period or deletion procedure exists for poll_responses, published CSVs, or voter-file numbers loaded into Twilio, and no removal path exists for residents who ask.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention period or deletion procedure for poll_responses, published CSVs, or voter-file numbers.

attacks.claim: Drag-to-rank is the primary named interaction, and keyboard and screen-reader ranking is deferred to a one-week pass in week 5, too late to shape the week-2 UI. SMS outreach has no accessible-format consideration.
attacks.evidence: "drag or tap-to-rank" and "Week 5: accessibility pass"

attacks.claim: Authoring, mobile ranking, IRV, abuse controls, open-data export, staff PDF, and SMS pipeline fit five weeks for three people with no cut line; the riskiest parts (abuse controls, export, SMS) are the most likely to be rushed.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: IRV tally, results page, abuse controls." / "Week 4: open-data export, staff PDF, voter-file import + SMS pipeline."

attacks.claim: No owner is named to author or approve poll options, and no pre-launch review of the content residents see as official input is required before messages go to ~142,000 people.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: poll-authoring and approval authority; "Council staff get the same CSV plus a PDF summary emailed Monday 07:00."

attacks.claim: Publishing advisory polls on agenda items and emailing PDFs to staff may raise public-records and open-meetings questions. No legal or records review is scheduled.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: legal, records-office, or open-meetings review in sections 6 or 7 timeline.

attacks.claim: All outreach depends on Twilio, with personal mobile numbers sent to a single third party and no residency or exit path stated.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio"
